topic: What if you acted like GTA 6 in real life for 24 hours?

script.text: Five p.m. A police car pulls up at the end of the street. And every game instinct you have says the same thing. Run.
So you run. For ten seconds. Then, as you already know, your legs quit.

And here's something the game never tells you. Running from the police doesn't make things go away. In a lot of places, running from an officer is a crime all by itself. You just turned a few tickets into something much bigger.
You crawl into a hedge behind the library. Rule five. Hide. Wait for the stars to fade.
Here's the problem. Real police don't have stars. They have dogs.
A police dog has up to three hundred million scent receptors in its nose. You have about six million. To a dog, you're not hiding. You're a big, sweaty, hot-dog-scented sign that says, 'Here.'
And there's a helicopter. Its thermal camera doesn't care about the hedge. It sees your body heat glowing like a light bulb.
In the game, you hide behind a dumpster and the helicopter flies right past. In real life, the pilot just says, 'Hedge behind the library,' into the radio.
The dog's name is Biscuit. Biscuit finds you in forty seconds, sits down next to the hedge, and wags his tail like he just won a prize.
Eight minutes. That's how long rule five lasts.
An officer parts the leaves and looks down at you. 'Are you the one from the video?'

science.claim: A dog's nose has up to 300 million scent receptors; a human's about 6 million.
science.working: Commonly cited figures: dogs up to 300 million olfactory receptors (breed dependent), humans about 5-6 million.
science.source: PBS NOVA, 'Dogs' Dazzling Sense of Smell' (2012)

science.claim: A police helicopter's thermal camera sees body heat through bushes.
science.working: Forward-looking infrared (FLIR) cameras detect the infrared heat a 37 °C body gives off against a cooler background; thin foliage does not hide it.
science.source: Police air support practice, e.g. UK National Police Air Service
